video_title: Is Ethereum Losing Its Last Edge?
gist: Blockworks Research analysts put 80-95% odds on the BTC bottom (~$58k) being in, citing ETF flows and under-allocated wealth managers, and argue DATs are a dying, access-arbitrage trade. The core of the episode is a debate: Carlos argues Ethereum's last moat (liquidity in stablecoins/lending) is slowly eroding because tokenized equities, flagship apps (Uniswap, Aave, Ethena) and new products are growing on Robinhood Chain, Base, Solana and others, while Jake counters with ETH's still-dominant stablecoin/DeFi TVL share, a growing pie, and monetary premium; the episode closes on the CFTC's advance notice tying retail leverage to federal oversight of custodial spot trading.

insights.claim: Carlos sees the market in a BTC-led regime where BTC should outperform short term, and wants a breakout above the ~$87,000 resistance before the rally can expand into altcoins.
insights.speaker: Carlos
insights.so_what: Watch $87k as the trigger level for rotating from BTC into alts.
insights.quote: I think we're in a BTC le regime. Um, I think uh BTC would outperform in the short term

insights.claim: Jake puts a 90-95% probability on the Bitcoin bottom having been set around $58,000, with BTC still roughly 32% below its all-time high set about a year earlier, and expects a grind rather than a straight line back to highs.
insights.speaker: Jake
insights.so_what: Defines $58k as the invalidation level for the new-bull-market thesis; residual risk framed as black swans (US housing crash, a Russian plague outbreak).
insights.quote: I'm thinking maybe a 90 95% chance that the bottom was in around [clears throat] 58,000 Bitcoin was the bottom

insights.claim: Carlos is about 80% confident the bottom is in, and says the longer BTC holds current levels the less likely it is that this is a bear-market rally; positive ETF flows in August and September came even though Strategy bought little Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: Carlos
insights.so_what: ETF demand is absorbing supply without Strategy as the marginal buyer, which suggests broader underlying demand.

insights.claim: The host argues a US housing-market crisis would not be a true tail risk for BTC because it would force interest-rate cuts, which he sees as bullish for Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: Mark (host)
insights.so_what: Reframes a macro shock as a potential liquidity tailwind for BTC rather than a downside catalyst.
insights.quote: a housing market crisis I think forces interest rate cuts which could only be bullish for BTC

insights.claim: Futures and options open interest spiked in the third week of September and then unwound, but BTC price fell much less than leverage did, which the host reads as healthier, less leveraged price support.
insights.speaker: Mark (host)
insights.so_what: Price holding while leverage flushes is a constructive positioning signal.

insights.claim: On an RSI-versus-weekly-BTC-flows chart, BTC was in the overheated top-right zone during September but has pulled back to a less extended, neutral-to-bullish position over the past week.
insights.speaker: Mark (host)
insights.so_what: Suggests room to run without the market being stretched.

insights.claim: The host views ETFs as price followers rather than price setters, but still a good sentiment gauge; his data places BTC ETFs in an accumulation phase.
insights.speaker: Mark (host)
insights.so_what: Use ETF flows to confirm trend and sentiment, not to predict turns.
insights.quote: they tend to be price followers and not necessarily price setters

insights.claim: Large US financial institutions recommend a median 1-3% Bitcoin portfolio allocation (up over time from about 0.1%), and the host's rough 13F-based math suggests clients are only 10-20% of the way to the low end of those recommendations.
insights.speaker: Mark (host)
insights.so_what: Implies a multi-x structural bid from wealth-management channels if allocations converge to recommendations.
insights.quote: they're about 10 to 20% of the way to their low end of their recommendations

insights.claim: Bitcoin treasury company flows turned to net outflows in July due to Strategy selling, and in September Strategy sold common stock but was not the largest buyer: Strive was the largest purchaser.
insights.speaker: Mark (host)
insights.so_what: Strategy is no longer the reliable marginal BTC buyer; treasury flows have become a weaker source of demand.
insights.quote: Strive was the largest purchaser

insights.claim: Jake and Carlos see DATs as a trade that existed because of limited market access (e.g., the closed-end Grayscale trust traded at a deep discount); now that banks recommend 1-7% allocations and some brokerages offer direct BTC, they don't expect DATs to regain their highs.
insights.speaker: Jake
insights.so_what: Avoid DAT equities as a structural play; the access premium that justified them is gone.
insights.quote: I just I don't see them coming back from their all-time highs

insights.claim: Carlos argues most investors are better off owning the underlying asset or a spot ETF that tracks it one-to-one than playing mNAV games, though deep-discount DATs with a strong underlying protocol can pay off, citing Ethena's DAT StablecoinX trading around 0.1x mNAV before an ~8-10x move.
insights.speaker: Carlos
insights.so_what: The only DAT setup worth considering is a steep mNAV discount combined with improving protocol fundamentals.
insights.quote: I think most investors ers are probably just better off buying the the underlying

insights.claim: With Grayscale now offering a Zcash ETF, Carlos would choose the ETF over Zcash DAT Cypherpunk Technologies, since a DAT adds the risk of the vehicle falling even more when ZEC falls.
insights.speaker: Carlos
insights.so_what: New single-asset ETFs undercut the reason to hold the matching DATs.

insights.claim: Jake gives only two reasons to hold a DAT: arbitraging an mNAV discount, or betting the DAT narrative comes back and reprices them on narrative rather than fundamentals; he doubts the second will happen.
insights.speaker: Jake
insights.so_what: Treat DATs as discount-arb or narrative trades, not long-term holds.

insights.claim: The host, a former ETF-issuer employee, expects only a few DATs to survive and says Strategy has many levers (several preferred securities, convertibles, common stock, issuance and buybacks) that give it operating leverage.
insights.speaker: Mark (host)
insights.so_what: Concentrate any DAT exposure in the largest, most capital-flexible names.

insights.claim: The host predicts consolidation in which larger DATs acquire smaller ones trading at very low mNAV, giving the sector a missing exit mechanism and helping close mNAV discounts through better market efficiency.
insights.speaker: Mark (host)
insights.so_what: Deep-discount small DATs could become takeover targets; M&A is a catalyst for closing discounts.
insights.quote: when we start to see larger um dots acquire smaller dots because of that extremely low MNAV

insights.claim: The host favors ETH treasuries like BitMine and SharpLink, and some ETFs including Grayscale's, because they use part of management fees or staking revenue to fund protocol development and earn yield beyond simply holding.
insights.speaker: Mark (host)
insights.so_what: DATs on staking-capable assets have a revenue source that BTC-only treasuries lack.

insights.claim: The host questions why Strategy has not used option selling as an operating lever and says he has never heard Michael Saylor give a reason against it.
insights.speaker: Mark (host)
insights.so_what: A possible future source of Strategy yield and catalyst to watch.
insights.quote: I do think strategy should be looking at option selling

insights.claim: The host observes that tokenized on-chain index products (Index Coop, DeFi Pulse) never built liquidity because crypto users don't want diversification; they want more risk.
insights.speaker: Mark (host)
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of crypto basket and index products gaining traction with native users.
insights.quote: I don't I don't think crypto people really like diversification. I think they just want more and more risk.

insights.claim: ETH staking hit an all-time high of 36% of supply and has risen every month even though ETH price is down about 9% year to date, driven mainly by ETFs and treasury companies staking to offset roughly 2% annual inflation.
insights.speaker: Jake
insights.so_what: Staking growth reflects institutional holding behavior, not net-new demand.
insights.quote: we hit 36% um of all ETH being staked

insights.claim: Jake says rising staking lowers ETH's liquid float, which can amplify price moves in both directions because exiting stakers face a queue, but it does not create net new buyers.
insights.speaker: Jake
insights.so_what: Expect higher ETH volatility; good for short-term traders, less so for long-term holders.
insights.quote: it's not creating net new buyers so there's less ETH available to sell

insights.claim: EIP-8363, which would have removed ETH yield and issuance once 50% of supply was staked (around mid-2028 at the current pace), was pulled from inclusion and given its own six-month process, so the roughly 2.5% staking yield is safe for now.
insights.speaker: Jake
insights.so_what: Removes near-term risk to validator and LST yields; the proposal may come back next year.

insights.claim: About 15 million ETH sits in liquid staking tokens, against roughly 1-1.1 million ETH of net new issuance per year.
insights.speaker: Jake
insights.so_what: Sizes the LST market and the dilution unstaked holders absorb.

insights.claim: Carlos disputes the idea that staking yield drives institutional ETH demand, arguing nobody buys an asset for 2% when it can move 50% in a year, and that the yield isn't even among the top three reasons to own ETH.
insights.speaker: Carlos
insights.so_what: Don't underwrite institutional ETH flows on the staking-yield narrative.
insights.quote: I don't think anybody buys ETH because it's giving you 2% uh yield uh when you can get a 50% draw down or a 50% increase

insights.claim: The host supported cutting issuance, arguing a deflationary or decreasing-supply asset (like buyback models at Pump.fun and Hyperliquid) is more attractive than a slightly higher staking yield, and that the staking yield is a subsidy for lending protocols that should be removed to force real product-market fit.
insights.speaker: Mark (host)
insights.so_what: Issuance cuts would pressure ETH-collateral lending loops but could strengthen ETH's value-accrual narrative.
insights.quote: I think the staking yields is a is a subsidy on the lending sector

insights.claim: Jake says ETH's staking yield is effectively about zero in real terms because supply inflation offsets it, and as a holder he would prefer ETH to be deflationary.
insights.speaker: Jake
insights.so_what: Staking is defensive, mainly to avoid dilution; it is not a source of real return.

insights.claim: Carlos argues Ethereum has already lost the trading race to Solana and Hyperliquid, and that its remaining moat (stablecoin and lending liquidity) is slowly eroding: not through a mass exodus, but because new growth happens elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Carlos
insights.so_what: Core bear case for ETH's relative performance against faster chains.
insights.quote: I think that mode like is starting to maybe slowly disappear

insights.claim: In tokenized equities, the volume race is between Base, Solana, Robinhood Chain and BNB, and Ethereum is not even competing; Carlos thinks the sector could follow stablecoins' path from zero to about $300 billion and could even end up larger.
insights.speaker: Carlos
insights.so_what: The marginal dollar in the next big on-chain category may bypass Ethereum L1.
insights.quote: it's not that Ethereum is losing the race. It's is that it's it's not even competing it

insights.claim: Tokenized equity issuers are mostly exchanges (Binance, Coinbase, Robinhood, Backpack), and each has an incentive to launch stocks on its own chain and grow liquidity there, which structurally disadvantages Ethereum.
insights.speaker: Carlos
insights.so_what: Exchange-owned chains capture tokenized equity activity; favor exposure to those ecosystems.

insights.claim: Aave, which Carlos calls Ethereum's most successful application, launched a Base equities hub with Coinbase, so growth in tokenized equity collateral will benefit Aave on Base rather than on Ethereum and reduce its reliance on the L1 over time.
insights.speaker: Carlos
insights.so_what: Aave can grow while ETH L1 does not; separate app exposure from chain exposure.

insights.claim: Most of Uniswap's 30-day volume now comes from Robinhood Chain; its growth had stagnated for years until that success, so Carlos thinks the Uniswap team will logically focus there rather than on Ethereum.
insights.speaker: Carlos
insights.so_what: UNI's growth driver is now Robinhood Chain, not Ethereum L1.

insights.claim: Ethereum L1's share of Ethena's USDe supply fell to 56% from 88% at last year's supply peak, as Ethena expands to Robinhood Chain, Base, Solana (via Kamino and Jupiter Lend), Plasma and Tron, and launched its neobank Ethena Pay on Avalanche rather than Ethereum.
insights.speaker: Carlos
insights.so_what: Even ETH-branded flagship apps put new products on other chains, a leading indicator of liquidity migration.
insights.quote: today 56% of USD supply uh is on the is on the Ethereum mill one compared to 88% back uh last year

insights.claim: Ethereum's tokenized equity supply ranks second only to BNB, but Carlos finds it is highly concentrated (around 60 wallets hold over 80%, largely Ondo) and mostly idle; the only real DeFi use he found is Saturn's SDRC used in a Pendle product.
insights.speaker: Carlos
insights.so_what: Headline tokenized-supply figures for Ethereum overstate real usage.

insights.claim: Of about 68k tokenized equity holder positions on Ethereum, 85% are worth under $1 and only about 1,500 exceed $10k, which Carlos says undercuts the claim that Ethereum tokenization is expanding global access.
insights.speaker: Carlos
insights.so_what: Retail global-access adoption is not yet visible on-chain.
insights.quote: 85% of those 68 uh K holder positions are worth under $1

insights.claim: Carlos argues payments are a loss leader and nearly all crypto protocol revenue comes from trading, so volume, not supply, is the key metric for tokenized equities.
insights.speaker: Carlos
insights.so_what: Value chains and apps by trading volume captured, not by assets parked on them.
insights.quote: revenue generating protocols in crypto it's basically all trading

insights.claim: Ethereum's stablecoin supply peaked at about $175B last year and is down to about $150B, while Hyperliquid, Solana, BNB, Robinhood Chain and Tron are at or near all-time highs, so Carlos expects a slow bleed in ETH dominance as the marginal dollar goes elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Carlos
insights.so_what: Track chain-level stablecoin supply trends as the leading indicator of where liquidity is moving.
insights.quote: It's probably going to be more of a slow bleed

insights.claim: Carlos concedes that every past call for Ethereum losing stablecoin dominance was wrong, so this is the part of his thesis where he has the least confidence; about 50% of ETH stablecoin supply sits on exchanges and is likely sticky.
insights.speaker: Carlos
insights.so_what: The stablecoin-dominance leg of the ETH bear case has a poor historical track record.
insights.quote: every other time that people said that Ethereum is going to lose like its stable coin dominance they were wrong

insights.claim: Carlos accepts that ETH carries a monetary premium (without it ETH would be the most overvalued asset on earth) but expects that premium to compress over time, with marginal dollars flowing to undervalued revenue-generating apps like Pump.fun and Hyperliquid.
insights.speaker: Carlos
insights.so_what: Rotate from L1 monetary-premium bets toward revenue-backed tokens.
insights.quote: if it didn't have like any monetary premium, it would be the most overvalued asset on on planet earth

insights.claim: Carlos says monetary-premium compression is also a problem for Solana and other low-revenue L1s, but Solana has a more credible path to justify its valuation through its trading activity and spot dominance.
insights.speaker: Carlos
insights.so_what: Relative-value lean: SOL over ETH on revenue growth potential.

insights.claim: The host contrasts Ethereum's 12-second block times (heading to 10 seconds next year after a planned 8-second target slipped) and a gas limit rising to 200 million with roughly 150 ms on Solana under Alpenglow, a gap of multiple orders of magnitude.
insights.speaker: Mark (host)
insights.so_what: Ethereum L1 cannot compete for latency-sensitive trading flow on its current roadmap.

insights.claim: Carlos doubts that cutting latency to around 4 seconds matters, and suggests Ethereum lean into liquidity and equity-collateral lending, or try charging L2s more to test its pricing power.
insights.speaker: Carlos
insights.so_what: Ethereum testing L2 fees or a fee switch would be a major value-capture catalyst to watch.
insights.quote: let's start charging the L2s more

themes.theme: Ethereum bull rebuttal and value capture

insights.claim: Jake argues tokenized equities don't need volume to matter because their main use is global access: people in developing nations can simply hold S&P 500 or Apple exposure, so supply is also a meaningful metric.
insights.speaker: Jake
insights.so_what: A buy-and-hold use case would favor whichever chain is trusted for settlement over the one with the most trading.

insights.claim: Ethereum still holds 48% of total stablecoin market cap (about $307B total), down from 53% two years ago and 60% three years ago, and its share of DeFi TVL is 56%, within a 54-60% range since 2022.
insights.speaker: Jake
insights.so_what: ETH's DeFi TVL share is stable even as its stablecoin share slowly declines.

insights.claim: Jake argues stablecoins aren't winner-take-all: if total supply grows to about $3 trillion within five years, Ethereum could fall to 30% share yet grow from about $147B to roughly $1 trillion in stablecoin supply.
insights.speaker: Jake
insights.so_what: ETH can lose dominance and still grow in absolute terms; Carlos replies that this is relatively more bullish for other chains.
insights.quote: stable coins is not winner take all like the the whole pie can grow and everyone can win

insights.claim: Jake argues that Robinhood Chain, Arbitrum and Base are Ethereum L2s, so Ethereum should earn a premium from activity built on them even without fees, and that L1s carry a monetary premium (the 'world computer' idea) that makes revenue matter less.
insights.speaker: Jake
insights.so_what: The ETH bull case leans on monetary premium and the L2 ecosystem, not fee revenue.

insights.claim: Carlos calls the 'L2s are built on Ethereum' argument cope, since activity moving to L2s sends little economic value to the L1, and says he will hold that view until the data shows otherwise.
insights.speaker: Carlos
insights.so_what: L2 growth should not be counted as ETH value accrual without fee evidence.
insights.quote: I just think that's kind of like cope

insights.claim: Jake estimates ETH trades at roughly 1,000x FDV to revenue on a ~$330B market cap, so it must carry a monetary premium; without one, all L1s would fall about 90%.
insights.speaker: Jake
insights.so_what: L1 valuations depend on narrative-driven monetary premium, a key fragility.

insights.claim: Jake suggests Ethereum could follow an 'Amazon playbook': gather market share and L2s now, then turn on a fee switch later (e.g., 1% of transactions), which would generate large revenue though it would be poorly received.
insights.speaker: Jake
insights.so_what: Optionality on future L1 value capture is an underpriced upside scenario for ETH.

insights.claim: The host sees a strong correlation between L1 prices and daily active users, DEX volume and revenue (especially DEX volume), calls it pathetic that Ethereum is nowhere on the DEX volume leaderboard, and believes Ethereum's L1 premium is shrinking.
insights.speaker: Mark (host)
insights.so_what: Use DEX volume share as the key fundamental input for L1 relative value.

themes.theme: CFTC advance notice on crypto exchanges

insights.claim: On October 5 the CFTC issued an advance notice (with a 60-day comment period, not yet a proposed rule): if an exchange offers leverage to retail, all of its custodial spot trading would fall under CFTC rules until coins are withdrawn, via a new opt-in crypto-only federal exchange license; exchanges without margin stay under state licenses.
insights.speaker: Jake
insights.so_what: Gives Coinbase and Kraken a path to offer retail leverage and run exchange, broker and clearing under one roof, a potential revenue catalyst.
insights.quote: if an exchange offers leverage to retail users, all of its custodial spot trading would then fall under CFTC rules until coins are withdrawn to the users's wallets

insights.claim: Under the CFTC notice, DeFi would likely stay outside the rules because on-chain trades settle directly to user wallets, but custodial staking would take a hit, as the CFTC suggests customers may need to be able to stake without intermediary fees.
insights.speaker: Jake
insights.so_what: A risk to exchange staking-fee revenue; a relative tailwind for non-custodial DeFi.

insights.claim: The CFTC moved because the Senate stalled the Clarity Act; regulatory rules are weaker than legislation and could be reversed by a future CFTC or administration. Chair Michael Selig framed the effort around consumer protection after FTX.
insights.speaker: Jake
insights.so_what: Regulatory gains are not durable; market-structure legislation remains the key unresolved risk.
